svg.title: Synchronization state: where the token is stored decides what a crash costs
svg.desc: Three ways to store the token relative to the data, each with a crash at the worst moment. Variant A, token first: the consumer saves the new token, then applies the changes; a crash after saving the token and before applying means the next run asks from the new token, so the changes of that batch are never applied; the copy is silently wrong. Variant B, data first, token after: the consumer applies the changes, then saves the token; a crash in between means the next run asks from the old token and receives the same changes again; this is safe only if applying is idempotent, which upsert by id and delete by id are. Variant C, one transaction: changes and token are committed together; a crash before the commit leaves old data and old token, a crash after leaves new data and new token; there is no in-between state. Variant C is used when the target has transactions, as the SQLite database of this lesson does; variant B with an idempotent apply is the rule when the target is another system without a shared transaction. Below, four more parts of the state: one token per table and per consumer; the time of the last successful run, to detect a token older than the tracking window; a full reload path that replaces the copy; and a comparison of row counts as a reconciliation.
